why.catColor: Affects users with low vision, color blindness, or anyone in bright or dim lighting conditions.
why.catAria: Affects screen reader users - ARIA communicates role, state, and properties to assistive technology.
why.catForms: Affects all users filling out forms, especially screen reader users and people with cognitive disabilities.
why.catKeyboard: Affects keyboard-only users and people using switches, head wands, or eye-tracking input.
why.catLanguage: Affects screen reader users - incorrect language settings cause mispronunciation.
why.catNameRoleValue: Affects screen reader users - elements need proper names, roles, and values to be understood by assistive technology.
why.catSemantics: Affects screen reader users navigating by landmarks, headings, and element types.
why.catSensoryVisualCues: Affects low-vision and color-blind users who cannot rely on visual cues alone.
why.catStructure: Affects screen reader users relying on heading hierarchy and landmark regions to navigate the page.
why.catTextAlternatives: Affects blind and low-vision users who rely on text descriptions of images, icons, and non-text content.
why.catTimeMedia: Affects users with cognitive disabilities, people who are deaf or hard-of-hearing, and anyone who needs more time to consume content.
why.wcagLevelA: WCAG Level A - the most basic web accessibility features. Failure means some users cannot use the page at all.
why.wcagLevelAA: WCAG Level AA - addresses the most common barriers for users with disabilities. Required by most accessibility regulations.
why.wcagLevelAAA: WCAG Level AAA - the highest standard, ensuring the best possible experience for all users.
why.bestPractice: Not a formal WCAG requirement, but a strongly recommended practice for an inclusive user experience.
why.principle1: WCAG Principle 1 - Perceivable. Content must be presented in ways all users can perceive. Affects blind, low-vision, deaf, and hard-of-hearing users.
why.principle2: WCAG Principle 2 - Operable. Interface components must be usable by everyone. Affects keyboard-only users, motor-impaired users, and people using alternative input devices.
why.principle3: WCAG Principle 3 - Understandable. Content and operation must be clear. Affects people with cognitive disabilities, learning difficulties, and non-native speakers.
why.principle4: WCAG Principle 4 - Robust. Content must work with current and future assistive technologies.

onboarding.title: Getting started with AccessLab
onboarding.subtitle: A four-step tour of the studio: pick an element, shape it, watch the live audit react, and learn as you go.

welcome.heading:
The intuitive way to learn
web accessibility
welcome.body: AccessLab is a hands-on space for developers of every level. Pick a UI element, adjust parameters or styling, and watch WCAG 2.2 accessibility issues surface in real time. Every change shows you how it helps, or hinders, the people who use it.

pick.lead: Pick from a list of real, browser-native HTML elements.

sidebar.title: Pick an HTML element to audit
sidebar.description: Choose from a list of elements in the options menu on the left.

variant.title: Choose a variant
variant.description: Many elements offer variants. Open the Markup picker to change how the element is written.

tune.lead: Make adjustments. Every edit re-runs the audit instantly.

controls.title: Adjust in controls panel
controls.description: Edit the label, colours, size, ARIA, state and more. The live preview and generated code update as you type.

counts.title: Live issue counts
counts.description: A running count of critical issues, warnings and passing checks update instantly.

issues.title: Issues, explained
issues.description: The Issues tab lists every finding with its WCAG level, why it matters, and how to fix it.

learn.lead: Understand the why - and take the code with you.

learn.title: Learn as you work
learn.description: The Learn tab holds short, plain-language articles on each topic. Articles relevant to the current element are pinned to the top.

code.title: Generated code drawer
code.description: The drawer at the bottom shows the live HTML, CSS and JavaScript for your element. Copy it, and drop accessibility-compatible code directly into your project.

issue.title: Elements must meet minimum colour contrast
issue.description: The text/background pair resolves to 3.1:1, below the 4.5:1 minimum.

learn.title: Why button type matters
learn.summary: A button with no type defaults to submit inside a form.
